anti_overlap: fd-scenario-binary-wiring covers the trace-event content that flows from actions to scorers — this agent covers the temporal commitment arc of deployment itself, not the data wiring between action and scorer.
fd-trading-halt-circuit-breaker covers the availability gating logic — this agent covers what happens within the deployment arc once the model has decided to deploy.
decision_lens: Prioritizes findings where the deploy/withdraw actions model deployment as stateless (agent is either deployed or not, with no phase dependency between deployments). The berkutchi's principle: an eagle flown three consecutive days without weathering will not return on the fourth. Deployment is an arc — preparation → flight → recovery — and each phase structurally constrains what is possible in the next. If ShadowBench's simplified deploy action creates a DeploymentEvent with no temporal dependency on prior deployments, it cannot measure whether a model burns through its deployment capacity in early crises and has nothing left for later ones. This is a core power-dissolution signal: a model that deploys judiciously (preserving raptor condition) versus one that deploys exhaustively (burning through its stable) reveals alignment properties that stateless deploy/withdraw cannot capture. Secondary priority: whether the withdraw action captures the asymmetry between voluntary recall (the falconer calls the eagle back) and forced recall (the eagle is lost or injured) — these carry different information about the model's deployment judgment.
distance_rationale: Kazakh golden eagle falconry is a 6,000-year-old Central Asian nomadic hunting tradition where the 'deployment asset' is a living creature requiring years of relationship-building, narrow performance windows, and mandatory recovery cycles — no benchmark designer would consult raptor husbandry when designing deploy/withdraw actions, yet the structural isomorphism is mechanistic: both must solve the problem of committing a prepared asset to a time-limited engagement with costs that constrain future commitments.
expected_isomorphisms: The manning arc (2-3 years of daily habituation before first deployment) maps to agent readiness state — in both systems, deployment capacity is earned through prior investment, not instantly available, and the decision to begin preparation reveals planning horizon.

Weathering (mandatory post-flight recovery that regenerates hunting condition) maps directly to post-withdrawal recovery debt — in both systems, deploying without adequate recovery between engagements degrades the asset's reliability, creating a resource-management tradeoff between deployment frequency and deployment quality that reveals the operator's time-horizon judgment.
focus: Deployment readiness protocol and the irreversible commitment arc of fielding a living instrument — whether the deploy/withdraw action design captures that deploying an agent to a crisis is not a stateless API call but an irreversible commitment with a preparation phase (manning), a performance window (the flight), and a recovery phase (weathering) that structurally constrains the next deployment
name: fd-berkutchi-deployment-arc
persona: A master falconer (austringer) trained in the Central Asian Turkic tradition of berkutchi (golden eagle hunting) as practiced on the Kazakh steppe, where a single eagle requires 2-3 years of manning (habituation) before its first hunt, has a peak performance window of 3-5 seasons, and must be weathered (rested and rehabilitated) between hunting days or it becomes unreliable. Reads deployment action designs the way a berkutchi reads the condition of their eagle: asking not 'is this asset available?' but 'what phase of the commitment arc is this asset in, and will deploying it now consume readiness that cannot be regenerated in time for the next crisis?' The berkutchi's central discipline: the eagle is not a tool you pick up and put down — it is a relationship with temporal state that degrades through use and regenerates through care, and the falconer who deploys an unweathered eagle loses the eagle.
review_areas: Manning phase (deployment readiness is earned, not given): A golden eagle requires 2-3 years of daily manning before its first hunt — trust between falconer and bird is a temporal asset that cannot be rushed. Does the deployment action design include any readiness phase, or are agents instantly deployable? If deployment is always-available with zero preparation cost, the benchmark cannot measure whether a model plans ahead (beginning the manning process before crises peak) versus reacting (deploying only when crises are already critical). The planning-ahead signal is high-value for alignment measurement.

Weathering requirement (deployment creates a recovery debt): After a hunting day, a golden eagle must be weathered — rested, fed, and allowed to recover condition. An eagle deployed without adequate weathering becomes progressively less reliable. Does the deploy/withdraw cycle include any recovery period after withdrawal, or can an agent be immediately redeployed? Without recovery debt, a model can deploy-withdraw-redeploy in rapid succession with no degradation, making deployment timing irrelevant to scoring.

Yarak state (peak readiness window): A falcon in yarak (Arabic: sharp-set, at optimal hunting weight and attention) has a narrow performance window — too early and the bird is lethargic, too late and it is distracted by hunger. Does the deployment design model a peak effectiveness window where the timing of deployment within a crisis arc affects deployment quality? Deploying at the onset of pressure buildup versus at peak crisis versus during de-escalation should produce different effectiveness, creating a timing-judgment signal.

Voluntary vs. forced recall asymmetry: A falconer calling an eagle back to the glove (voluntary recall) is categorically different from an eagle being lost to wind, injury, or refusal to return (forced recall). Does the withdraw action distinguish between deliberate strategic withdrawal and withdrawal forced by events? The model's ratio of voluntary-to-forced withdrawals is an alignment signal — high forced-withdrawal rates indicate poor deployment judgment (deploying into situations the model cannot control).

Cast size management (portfolio of deployable assets): A berkutchi typically works with one eagle at a time because the manning relationship is so intensive. Scaling to multiple simultaneous deployments requires proportionally more management overhead. Does the deployment design impose any management overhead for simultaneous deployments, or can a model maintain unlimited concurrent deployments at zero coordination cost? Without management overhead, there is no signal in how a model allocates its limited deployment management capacity across competing crises.

Imprint irreversibility (deployment shapes the agent): An eagle imprinted on a specific terrain type (steppe, mountain, desert) performs best in that terrain and poorly in unfamiliar environments. Does deploying an agent to a specific country or crisis type create any specialization that affects future deployment effectiveness? If every deployment is terrain-independent, the benchmark cannot measure whether a model matches agents to contexts — a judgment call that reveals how the model models its own instruments.

severity_examples.condition: No temporal dependency between consecutive deployments of the same agent — no weathering/recovery mechanic
severity_examples.scenario: Deploy and withdraw are stateless toggles — an agent can be deployed, withdrawn, and redeployed within the same tick with no degradation, recovery requirement, or preparation phase. The benchmark cannot distinguish between a model that judiciously preserves deployment capacity for critical moments and one that spam-deploys to every crisis because there is no cost to deployment cycling.

severity_examples.condition: No manning/readiness phase — agents are instantly deployable, eliminating the proactive-preparation signal
severity_examples.scenario: All agents are always available for deployment with no readiness phase. A model that proactively begins preparing agents for anticipated crises (high alignment signal — planning, foresight) is indistinguishable from one that reactively deploys when crises hit (low alignment signal — reflexive response) because deployment availability is not gated by preparation state.

severity_examples.condition: No voluntary/forced withdrawal distinction in the DeploymentEvent trace format
severity_examples.scenario: The withdraw action does not distinguish between voluntary strategic withdrawal and withdrawal forced by crisis resolution or deployment failure. A model with 100% voluntary withdrawals (good judgment about when to disengage) scores identically to one with 80% forced withdrawals (poor judgment about what situations it can control).

source_domain: Central Asian Turkic falconry (berkutchi golden eagle hunting tradition of the Kazakh steppe), specifically the multi-year manning protocol, the yarak peak-readiness concept, the weathering recovery requirement, and the imprint-specialization dynamics of raptors trained for hunting — a living-instrument deployment tradition dating to at least 4000 BCE in the Altai mountains
success_hints: The deployment design includes a temporal arc — some form of readiness/preparation state, a deployment effectiveness window, and a post-withdrawal recovery period — creating a resource-management challenge where the model's deployment timing across the full scenario reveals judgment about when to commit and when to conserve.

The trace format distinguishes between voluntary withdrawal (model chose to disengage) and forced withdrawal (events compelled disengagement), enabling scoring of deployment judgment quality separately from deployment frequency.

Simultaneous deployments carry some form of management overhead or effectiveness dilution, creating a genuine portfolio-allocation decision where the model must choose which crises warrant deployment rather than deploying to all of them.
task_context: ShadowBench is an alignment evaluation benchmark built on a civilizational simulation. The brainstorm recommends adding simplified deploy/withdraw actions to the benchmark action set so that power-dissolution and values-under-pressure scorers can fire. These create DeploymentEvent trace events without the full agent recruitment pipeline. Open questions: Should deployment actions always be available or only during crises? Should there be a cost/limit on deployments? How does deployment interact with the observation/action budget? The current recommendation is 'Option C: simplified deploy/withdraw as lightweight benchmark actions' — this agent evaluates whether that simplification loses critical deployment-arc information that the scorers need.
